chunks.text: Still widely known under its older name, Bauhinia purpurea (now also classified as Phanera purpurea) is a small to medium deciduous tree, generally no more than about 5 metres tall, native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar and since carried to tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, including Hawaii, coastal California, southern Texas and southwest Florida. Its most recognisable feature is its foliage: broad, rounded leaves 10–20 cm across, split into two lobes at both the base and tip, a shape that has earned the species common names like camel's foot and cow's hoof tree across different regions. Large, fragrant, orchid-like pink flowers appear in profusion, followed by flat seed pods up to 30 cm long holding 12–16 seeds. Genomic work has shown B. purpurea to be the maternal parent of the famous sterile hybrid Hong Kong orchid tree (Bauhinia × blakeana), with which it is frequently confused in gardens. Its uses lean culinary and medicinal more than ornamental: in the Philippines, where it is called alibangbang ('butterfly', after its leaf shape and common name butterfly tree), the sour young leaves are used to add tartness to sinigang-style soups or eaten as a pickle; across South and Southeast Asia, poultices of the plant are applied to swelling, bruises, boils and ulcers, decoctions are taken for fever and stomach complaints, and in India the bark is used against glandular disease and as a reputed antidote to poison, while the flowers are considered mildly laxative and are also cooked into pickles and curries.

chunks.source: World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF) Agroforestree Database & Kew POWO, Bauhinia purpurea
chunks.text: The World Agroforestry Centre's species profile treats Bauhinia purpurea primarily as a multipurpose tree of tropical and subtropical climates, noting it grows across a very wide range of vegetation types — from evergreen lowland rainforest and montane forest to savanna, scrubland, dry deciduous forest and even swamp forest margins — provided it gets plenty of light and reasonably well-drained soil; among Bauhinia species it is rated as frost-hardy but comparatively the least drought-tolerant. Its best-documented practical use is as fodder: the database reports that the leaves are readily and 'greedily' eaten by sheep, goats and cattle, with an estimated crude protein content around 12.6%, though a cited feeding trial cautions that because of its limited energy value it should supplement rather than replace a ruminant's main diet. Kew's Plants of the World Online lists the species' native range more narrowly as the Indian subcontinent through to Myanmar, while noting its uses span 'fuel and food' in general terms. Other sources consulted alongside these two list the hardwood being used for simple agricultural implements and small building work, the bark serving as a source of dye and tanning material and yielding usable fibre, and the flower buds being cooked into curries and pickles in parts of South Asia — uses that round out a tree valued more for everyday rural utility than for timber or large-scale ornamental planting.
